question: Which statement best describes Route organization with groups?
options: Server Components are the default and should be the majority: they fetch data, keep secrets server-side, and ship no JS. Push 'use client' as LOW in the tree as possible — only the genuinely interactive leaves (a toggle, a form, a chart). Server Components can render Client Components and pass them server-fetched data as props, so you rarely need to make a whole page a client component.

Server Actions are the default for mutations driven by your own UI (form submits, button clicks) — they're colocated, typed, and integrate with revalidation. Route Handlers (app/api/.../route.ts) are for HTTP endpoints consumed by external clients, webhooks, mobile apps, or anything needing a stable URL, custom methods, or streaming. Use actions for app-internal mutations, handlers for a public/programmatic API.

Route groups — folders wrapped in parentheses like (marketing) or (app) — let you group routes by concern and give each its own layout WITHOUT adding a URL segment. You typically split a large app into a public marketing group, an authenticated app group, and an admin group, each with their own root layout, so concerns (and rendering strategies) don't bleed together.

Don't scatter fetch() calls across pages. Centralize reads in a data-access layer (e.g. lib/data/*) of typed functions that fetch and tag/revalidate their data, and that enforce auth/tenant scope. This gives you one place to set caching policy (revalidate, tags), to authorize access, and to mock in tests — keeping pages thin and consistent.

question: Which statement best describes The Server/Client boundary?
options: Keep route files (page/layout/loading/error) under app/, and put everything reusable outside it: components/ for UI, lib/ for data-access and utilities, and colocate route-specific pieces in a _components or actions.ts beside the route. A common convention is feature-first folders so a feature's UI, data, and actions live together, with truly shared code promoted to top-level dirs.

Next shines when you need SEO/SSR, a mix of static and dynamic pages, server-side data access, and a unified React full-stack. It's a poorer fit for a purely internal SPA with no SEO needs (a plain SPA is simpler), a heavy real-time/streaming backend (use a dedicated server), or a mostly-static site that a lighter SSG tool handles with less complexity. Match the tool to the actual rendering and backend needs.
